Thousands of Strangers Become Family at Chinese Groom’s Wedding

A 24-year-old Chinese man who feared his wedding would be almost empty ended up celebrating with thousands of strangers after a heartfelt social media invitation went viral.

Xu Chenghong, who lost his father at age three and his grandmother at seven, grew up with very few close family members. After years of hard work, he finally saved enough to marry his girlfriend, but feared that only a handful of guests would attend.

Hoping to make the day less lonely, he posted an invitation on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, asking strangers to join his wedding. He expected around 10 to 20 people to show up.

Instead, thousands of people reportedly travelled from across China to celebrate with the couple. Some brought livestock, food and household appliances, while volunteer chefs prepared meals and supporters helped organise the event. A Maybach was even arranged for the newlyweds.

The overwhelming response forced organisers to move the celebration to a larger venue, with local authorities helping manage the crowds.

What began as a simple request for a few wedding guests became an extraordinary celebration of kindness, proving that family is not always defined by blood, but by the people who show up when it matters most.

प्रधानमन्त्रीका प्रमुख सल्लाहकार कुमार बेनले आइतबार फेसबुकमा २८ जना पत्रकारको सूचीलाई लिएर व्यङ्ग्यात्मक टिप्पणी गरेपछि प्रधानमन्त्री बालेनले पनि त्यसमा प्रतिक्रिया दिएका हुन् ।

बेनले पत्रकारहरूलाई मेन्सन गर्दै लेखेका थिए, ‘यो २८ जना पत्रकारमा को–को पर्‍या हो ? २८ मा नपर्ने नि के पत्रकार भन्नु हैन साथी हो।’

उनको उक्त पोस्टमा प्रतिक्रिया दिँदै प्रधानमन्त्री बालेनले लेखेका छन्, ‘कुपण्डोल जाने मात्र पत्रकार, अरू कलाकार।’

पत्रकार पक्राउको घटनापछि सञ्चारमाध्यम र पत्रकारमाथि प्रहरीको धरपकडबारे सरकारसँग जवाफ मागिँदै आएको छ । यही पृष्ठभूमिमा प्रधानमन्त्री र उनका प्रमुख सल्लाहकारका व्यङ्ग्यात्मक टिप्पणी सार्वजनिक भएपछि विवाद थप चर्किने देखिएको छ ।

संविधानको धारा १९ ले सञ्चारको हक सुनिश्चित गरेको छ । त्यस्तै, सूचनाको हकसम्बन्धी ऐन, २०६४ ले समाचारको स्रोत गोप्य राख्न पाउने व्यवस्थासमेत गरेको छ । यस्तो अवस्थामा पत्रकार पक्राउ प्रकरणबारे सरकारको धारणा र जिम्मेवारीलाई लिएर बहस जारी छ ।

Too Much Screen Time in Schools? Sweden Is Changing Its Education Strategy

Sweden is rethinking its technology-driven education strategy after growing concerns about the impact of excessive screen use on children's learning. Once among the countries enthusiastically introducing laptops and tablets into classrooms, Sweden is now shifting its focus back towards printed textbooks, handwriting and traditional reading.

The change follows concerns over declining reading performance among fourth-grade students between 2016 and 2021. Educators and researchers have raised questions about children's concentration, reading comprehension and dependence on digital devices. In response, Sweden has invested more than 2.1 billion Swedish kronor in printed textbooks and teacher guides.

The country has also changed its approach to early childhood education, with preschools no longer required to use digital tools. More classroom time is being directed towards reading physical books and practising handwriting, while a nationwide mobile phone ban in schools is planned.

However, Sweden's shift does not mean completely rejecting technology. Digital skills remain important for children's future, but policymakers are increasingly recognising that screens are not necessarily the best learning tool for every age group or subject. The country's experience highlights an important lesson for education systems worldwide: technological innovation should support learning, not replace the fundamentals of reading, writing and focused attention.

Nepal Beats India, Pakistan and Bangladesh to Become South Asia’s Happiest Country

Nepal has emerged as South Asia’s highest-ranked country in the World Happiness Report 2026, securing 99th position among 147 countries with a happiness score of 5.147 out of 10. The ranking places Nepal ahead of Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, marking a notable achievement for the country in the global wellbeing assessment.

Finland has retained its position as the world’s happiest country for the ninth consecutive year, scoring 7.764. Iceland, Denmark, Costa Rica and Sweden followed in the top five, while Nordic countries once again dominated the rankings. The report is based on people's assessments of their overall quality of life, collected through the Gallup World Poll.

In South Asia, Pakistan ranked 104th, India 116th, Bangladesh 127th, Sri Lanka 134th and Afghanistan 147th, placing it at the bottom of the global list. Nepal’s leading regional position reflects its relatively stronger performance in areas such as social support and freedom to make life choices, although its overall score remains considerably lower than that of the world's happiest countries.

The report measures happiness through people's life evaluations and examines factors including income, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity and perceptions of corruption. While Nepal's regional ranking is encouraging, it does not mean the country is free from economic and social challenges. Improvements in employment, healthcare, education and governance remain essential to improving people's quality of life.

शनिबार सामाजिक सञ्जाल फेसबुकमार्फत आफ्नो धारणा सार्वजनिक गर्दै आईजीपी कार्कीले नेपाल प्रहरीले सञ्चारकर्मीबाट सधैँ निष्पक्ष र तथ्यमा आधारित पत्रकारिताको अपेक्षा राख्ने बताएका हुन्।

विभिन्न सञ्चारगृहबाट पत्रकार पक्राउ परेको घटनाको २४ घण्टा नबित्दै आईजीपी कार्कीको यस्तो धारणा सार्वजनिक भएको हो। पत्रकार पक्राउ र समाचार कक्षमा प्रहरी प्रवेशको प्रयासपछि प्रहरीको कार्यशैली तथा प्रेस स्वतन्त्रताबारे व्यापक आलोचना भइरहेको छ।

विभिन्न सञ्चारमाध्यमका पत्रकार पक्राउ परेको घटनापछि राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा) का सभापति रवि लामिछानेले पार्टीको सचिवालय बैठक बोलाएका छन्। समसामयिक राजनीतिक विषयमा छलफल गर्न शनिबार बिहान बैठक बस्न लागेको हो।

रास्वपाका प्रवक्ता जगदीश खरेलका अनुसार सभापति लामिछानेको अध्यक्षतामा बस्ने बैठक बिहान ११ बजे काठमाडौंको वनस्थलीस्थित पार्टीको केन्द्रीय कार्यालय घण्टीघरमा हुनेछ।

प्रहरीले पत्रकारहरूलाई पक्राउ गर्नुका साथै सञ्चारमाध्यमका कार्यालयमै पुगेर धरपकडको प्रयास गरेपछि यस विषयले राजनीतिक वृत्तमा समेत चर्चा पाएको छ। यही घटनाक्रमपछि सभापति लामिछानेले शुक्रबार राति नै पार्टीका नेताहरूलाई बैठकका लागि खबर पठाएका थिए।

बैठकमा पत्रकार पक्राउ प्रकरणलगायत समसामयिक विषयमा छलफल हुने प्रवक्ता खरेलले जानकारी दिएका छन्। तर, बैठकको विस्तृत कार्यसूची भने सार्वजनिक गरिएको छैन।

तीन पत्रकार पक्राउ परेको र काठमाडौंका विभिन्न सञ्चारमाध्यमका कार्यालयमा प्रहरी प्रवेश गर्ने प्रयास गरेको घटनामा व्यापक आलोचना भएपछि नेपाल प्रहरीले आफ्नो धारणा सार्वजनिक गरेको छ। प्रहरीले आफू प्रेस स्वतन्त्रता र पत्रकारको सुरक्षाप्रति प्रतिबद्ध रहेको बताउँदै पत्रकारहरूलाई पक्राउ गर्नुको सट्टा पछिल्लो समय प्रकाशित समाचारबारे छलफल गर्न बोलाइएको दाबी गरेको छ।

केन्द्रीय प्रहरी प्रवक्ता डीआईजी अविनारायण काफ्लेले सेतोपाटीसँग कुरा गर्दै सरकार र प्रहरी संगठनबीचको सम्बन्धबारे प्रकाशित समाचारका विषयमा पत्रकारहरूसँग छलफल गर्न खोजिएको बताएका छन्। उनका अनुसार केही समाचारले प्रहरीको व्यावसायिकता र अधिकृतहरूको कार्यसम्पादनप्रति अविश्वास सिर्जना गरेको तथा जनतामाझ नकारात्मक सन्देश प्रवाह गरेको प्रहरीको बुझाइ छ।

त्यस्ता समाचारले शान्ति सुरक्षा कायम गर्ने कार्यमा समेत असर पार्न सक्ने भन्दै साइबर ब्युरोले समाचारको तथ्य र त्यसको आधारबारे बुझ्न चाहेको काफ्लेले बताएका छन्।

यसअघि प्रहरीले नेपाल प्रेसको बानेश्वरस्थित कार्यालयबाट पत्रकार विश्वमणि सुवेदीलाई पक्राउ गरेको थियो। डीएनखबरका प्रधान सम्पादक धीरज बस्नेतलाई ईसेवा नम्बरसम्बन्धी विषयमा छलफल गर्ने भन्दै प्रहरी कार्यालय बोलाइएको र त्यसपछि नियन्त्रणमा लिइएको बताइएको छ। मोटिभेट न्युजका प्रधान सम्पादकलाई पनि प्रहरीले पक्राउ गरेको थियो।

प्रहरीले पक्राउ गरेका पत्रकारहरूलाई रिहा गरिसकेको छ। तर, समाचारबारे छलफल गर्न भन्दै पत्रकारहरूलाई किन पक्राउ गरियो र सञ्चारमाध्यमका समाचार कक्षमै प्रहरी किन पुग्यो भन्ने प्रश्न अझै उठिरहेको छ। घटनाले नेपालमा प्रेस स्वतन्त्रता, पत्रकारको सुरक्षा र प्रहरीको कार्यशैलीबारे गम्भीर बहस सिर्जना गरेको छ।

राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा) का संसदीय दलका सचेतक प्रकाशचन्द्र परियारले समाचारको विषयलाई लिएर पत्रकार पक्राउ गर्ने र सञ्चारमाध्यमका कार्यालयमै पुगेर धरपकडको प्रयास गर्ने प्रहरी शैलीप्रति कडा आपत्ति जनाएका छन्। उनले यस्तो गतिविधि तत्काल रोक्न र प्रेस स्वतन्त्रताको सम्मान गर्न सरकारसँग माग गरेका छन्।

शुक्रबार सामाजिक सञ्जाल फेसबुकमार्फत आफ्नो धारणा सार्वजनिक गर्दै परियारले पत्रकार विश्वमणि सुवेदी पक्राउ परेको घटना र नयाँ पत्रिकाको कार्यालयमा सादा पोसाकका प्रहरी पुगेको घटनाप्रति असन्तुष्टि जनाएका हुन्।

उनले प्रहरीको पछिल्लो कार्यशैलीलाई ‘पुलिस स्टेट’ अर्थात् ‘प्रहरी राज’ उन्मुख भएको टिप्पणी गरेका छन्। संविधानले सुनिश्चित गरेको प्रेस स्वतन्त्रताको संरक्षण र संवर्द्धन गर्नु राज्यको दायित्व भए पनि प्रहरीको यस्तो व्यवहार लोकतान्त्रिक राज्यको सामान्य चरित्रसँग मेल नखाने उनको भनाइ छ।

नयाँ पत्रिकाको कार्यालयमा पुगेका सादा पोसाकका प्रहरीको शैलीलाई ‘जंगे शैली’को संज्ञा दिँदै परियारले घटनालाई गम्भीर रूपमा लिनुपर्ने बताएका छन्।

उनले विदाको मुखमा भएको प्रहरी गतिविधिको छानबिन गर्न सरकारसँग विशेष मागसमेत गरेका छन्। साथै, पत्रकार तथा सञ्चारमाध्यमसँग सम्बन्धित विवाद र विषयलाई प्रहरीमार्फत नभई प्रेस काउन्सिलबाटै निरुपण गर्ने अभ्यास गर्नुपर्नेमा उनले जोड दिएका छन्।

परियारले प्रेस स्वतन्त्रताको सम्मान गर्दै सञ्चारमाध्यममाथि हुने प्रहरी हस्तक्षेप रोक्न सरकारको ध्यानाकर्षण गराएका छन्।

बङ्गालको खाडीमा विकसित चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’को अवशेष र पश्चिमी वायुको आंशिक प्रभावका कारण आज पनि देशका अधिकांश स्थानमा मौसम बदली रहने भएको छ। मौसम पूर्वानुमान महाशाखाका अनुसार कोशी, मधेस र बागमती प्रदेशका एक–दुई स्थानमा भारी वर्षा तथा हिमपातको सम्भावना रहेको छ।

हाल देशभर अधिकांश स्थानमा बादल लागेको छ। कोशी, मधेस, बागमती, गण्डकी र लुम्बिनी प्रदेशका धेरै स्थानमा मध्यम वर्षा भइरहेको छ भने कर्णाली र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशका केही स्थानमा हल्का वर्षा भइरहेको महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।

आज दिउँसो कोशी, मधेस, बागमती, गण्डकी, लुम्बिनी र कर्णाली प्रदेशमा अधिकांश बदली रहनेछ। सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशमा भने सामान्यतया बादल लाग्ने पूर्वानुमान छ। कोशी, मधेस र बागमतीका धेरै स्थानमा तथा गण्डकीका केही स्थानमा चट्याङसहित मध्यम वर्षा हुन सक्नेछ।

त्यस्तै, लुम्बिनी, कर्णाली र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशका हिमाली तथा पहाडी भूभागका केही स्थानमा पनि वर्षा र हिमपातको सम्भावना छ। विशेषगरी कोशी, मधेस र बागमती प्रदेशका एक–दुई स्थानमा भारी वर्षा तथा हिमपात हुन सक्ने महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।

आज राति पनि देशभर सामान्यतया बादल लाग्नेछ। हिमाली भूभागका थोरै स्थानमा मध्यम वर्षा र हिमपात हुन सक्नेछ भने कोशी र गण्डकी प्रदेशका पहाडी भूभागका एक–दुई स्थानमा हल्का वर्षाको सम्भावना रहेको छ।

आइतबार भने मौसममा क्रमिक सुधार आउने देखिएको छ। देशभर आंशिक बदली रहने र हिमाली तथा पहाडी भूभागका एक–दुई स्थानमा हल्का वर्षा तथा हिमपात हुन सक्ने महाशाखाको पूर्वानुमान छ।

चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’को अवशेष र पश्चिमी वायुको प्रभाव आज अपराह्नदेखि क्रमशः कमजोर हुँदै जाने महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।

विभिन्न सञ्चारमाध्यमका पत्रकारहरू पक्राउ परिरहेको घटनाबारे प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहको सचिवालयले आफूलाई कुनै जानकारी नभएको दाबी गरेको छ। प्रधानमन्त्री, उनको सचिवालय र प्रधानमन्त्री तथा मन्त्रिपरिषद् कार्यालयको यस घटनामा कुनै संलग्नता नरहेको सचिवालयले स्पष्ट पारेको छ।

प्रधानमन्त्रीका प्रेस तथा अनुसन्धान विज्ञ दीपा दाहालले आज विकसित घटनाक्रमबारे प्रधानमन्त्री र उनको कार्यालयलाई कुनै जानकारी नभएको बताएकी हुन्। अनलाइनखबरसँग कुरा गर्दै उनले पत्रकार पक्राउ गर्ने घटनामा प्रधानमन्त्री तथा उनको सचिवालयको कुनै भूमिका नरहेको दाबी गरिन्।

यसैबीच प्रहरीले विभिन्न सञ्चारमाध्यमका समाचार कक्षमै प्रवेश गरेर पत्रकारहरूलाई पक्राउ गरिरहेको छ। शुक्रबार नेपाल प्रेसमा कार्यरत पत्रकार विश्वमणि सुवेदी, डीएनखबरका पत्रकार धीरज बस्नेत र मोटिभेट न्युजका पत्रकार शोभराज बराल पक्राउ परेका छन्।

त्यस्तै, नयाँ पत्रिकामा कार्यरत पत्रकार नवराज मैनालीलाई पक्राउ गर्न सादा पोसाकमा खटिएका प्रहरीहरू पत्रिकाको कार्यालयमै पुगेका छन्। उनीहरूले मैनालीलाई आफूसँगै नलगी कार्यालय नछाड्ने भन्दै समाचार कक्षमै बसेको समाचारमा उल्लेख छ।

एकपछि अर्को सञ्चारमाध्यमका पत्रकार पक्राउ परेपछि प्रेस स्वतन्त्रता र समाचारको स्रोत संरक्षणको विषयमा गम्भीर प्रश्न उठेको छ। तर, प्रधानमन्त्री सचिवालयले भने घटनाबारे कुनै जानकारी नभएको र आफ्नो संलग्नता नरहेको बताएको छ।

बंगालको खाडीमा विकसित चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’ र पश्चिमी वायुको प्रभावले नेपालका अधिकांश भूभागमा वर्षा भइरहेको छ। कोशीदेखि गण्डकी प्रदेशसम्म शुक्रबार बिहानैदेखि झरी परेको छ भने वर्षा विस्तार हुँदै सुदूरपश्चिमसम्म पुगेको छ। काठमाडौं उपत्यकामा पनि रातिदेखि पानी पर्ने र रोकिने क्रम जारी छ।

जल तथा मौसम विज्ञान विभागका अनुसार पछिल्लो १२ घण्टामा कोशी प्रदेशका केही स्थानमा भारी वर्षा मापन भएको छ। धनकुटाको लेगुवाघाटमा ५२.८ मिलिमिटर र खोटाङको कुर्लेघाटमा ४८.२ मिलिमिटर वर्षा भएको छ। मौसमविद् रोजन लामिछानेका अनुसार न्यूनचापीय प्रणाली नेपालतर्फ अझै नजिकिँदै रहेकाले साँझपछि वर्षाको क्रम थप बढ्न सक्छ। विशेषगरी कोशी र बागमती प्रदेशका हिमाली क्षेत्रमा बढी वर्षा हुने सम्भावना छ।

त्रिभुवन विश्वविद्यालयका सहप्राध्यापक डा. विनोद पोखरेलले चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’को प्रभावले करिब ५ देखि १० घण्टासम्म भारी वर्षा हुन सक्ने बताएका छन्। यद्यपि वर्षाको समय, स्थान र मात्रा परिवर्तन हुन सक्ने भएकाले उनले साँझ र रातिको समयमा सतर्क रहन तथा आधिकारिक मौसम सूचना नियमित रूपमा हेर्न आग्रह गरेका छन्।

जापानका लागि प्रस्तावित नेपाली राजदूत जिज्ञान कुमार थापाबारे निर्णय लिन संसदीय सुनुवाइ समितिको बैठक आगामी सोमबार दिउँसो ३ बजे सिंहदरबारमा बस्ने भएको छ। सुनुवाइका क्रममा उठेका प्रश्नको चित्तबुझ्दो जवाफ र जापान सरकारबाट आवश्यक विवरण प्राप्त नभएपछि समितिले यसअघि उनको नाम अनुमोदन गर्ने वा नगर्ने निर्णय स्थगित गरेको थियो।

थापाको जापानको स्थायी बसोबास अनुमतिपत्र (पीआर), परिवारको पीआर, जापानमा रहेको घर–सम्पत्ति तथा त्यहाँको सरकारी निकायसँगको सम्बन्धबारे प्रश्न उठेको थियो। थापाले आफूले जापानको पीआर त्यागिसकेको बताए पनि उनकी श्रीमतीको पीआर कायमै रहेको र उनको नाममा जापानमा घरसमेत रहेको स्वीकार गरेका थिए। यसले राजदूत नियुक्तिमा स्वार्थ बाझिन सक्ने भन्दै समितिमा उजुरीसमेत परेको थियो।

यस विषयमा स्पष्ट जानकारी माग्दै समितिले परराष्ट्र मन्त्रालयमार्फत जापान सरकारसँग विवरण मागेको छ। तर, हालसम्म जापान सरकारबाट जवाफ प्राप्त भएको छैन। समितिले परराष्ट्र मन्त्रालयको रायसमेत लिएर यही कात्तिक १९ गतेभित्र थापाबारे अन्तिम निर्णय गर्ने तयारी गरेको छ।

संविधान तथा संसदीय सुनुवाइसम्बन्धी नियमअनुसार प्रस्तावित राजदूतको नाम प्राप्त भएको ४५ दिनभित्र समितिले निर्णय गर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ। कात्तिक १९ गते उक्त समयसीमा पूरा हुँदैछ। निर्धारित समयभित्र समितिले निर्णय दिन नसके थापाको नाम स्वतः अनुमोदन भएको मानिनेछ। त्यसैले सोमबारको बैठकलाई उनको राजदूत नियुक्तिको भविष्य निर्धारण गर्ने महत्वपूर्ण बैठकका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

A MOTHER WHALE AND HER CALF VANISHED AFTER SURVIVING A DANGEROUS JOURNEY

Snow Cone, a North Atlantic right whale, was entangled in fishing gear in March 2021. Rescue teams removed nearly 300 feet of rope, but some gear remained attached to her.

Despite her injuries, she traveled more than 1,300 miles and gave birth to a calf off the coast of Georgia on December 2, 2021.

Her calf was last reported sighted in April 2022, while Snow Cone has not been seen since October 2022. Their current whereabouts and fate remain unknown.

With only around 380 North Atlantic right whales remaining, every individual matters. Their story highlights the ongoing danger that fishing gear poses to this critically endangered species.

A WWII DESTROYER WAS FOUND MORE THAN 6,400 METRES UNDER THE OCEAN!

For decades, the USS Johnston rested in the darkness of the Philippine Sea, more than 6 kilometres beneath the surface.

The American destroyer sank on October 25, 1944, during the Battle off Samar in World War II. Despite facing a vastly larger Japanese force, the ship fought to protect vulnerable American escort carriers.

In 2019, explorers located wreckage believed to be the Johnston. But the mystery was finally solved in March 2021, when a crewed deep-sea submersible reached the main wreck at approximately 6,456 metres (21,180 feet).

The biggest confirmation?

The ship’s hull number 557 was still visible after more than 76 years underwater.

Of the 327 crew members, 141 survived.

Imagine discovering a ship resting in complete darkness, with its identity still written on its bow after all those years.

What other forgotten secrets could be waiting in the deepest parts of our oceans?

Former 75th Ranger Regiment sniper Nicholas Irving, known as "The Reaper," with his custom SR-25 sniper rifle, "Dirty Diana." Irving served as a sniper with 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment, and during a single deployment to Afghanistan in 2009, he was credited with 33 confirmed kills, one of the highest totals for a single deployment in special operations history.

The SR-25 was the rifle at the center of it all. A semi-automatic 7.62mm platform, it gave Ranger snipers the ability to engage multiple targets quickly at range, a critical advantage in the fast moving fights Rangers were known for. Irving named his "Dirty Diana," after the Michael Jackson song, and the rifle became almost as well known as the man behind it.

After leaving the Army, Irving told his story in his memoir, "The Reaper," and has spent the years since teaching marksmanship and sharing what he learned with a new generation of shooters.

Chief Special Warfare Operator (SEAL) Collin Trent Thomas, pictured downrange kitted up for high-threat direct-action raids across the Global War on Terror.

Enlisting in the U.S. Navy at age 19, Thomas initially completed training as a Hospital Corpsman before tackling the brutal crucible of BUD/S to earn his Trident. His relentless pursuit of excellence propelled him through the ranks, serving first with East Coast platoons at SEAL Team 4 and SEAL Team 2 before passing the grueling selection process for the Naval Special Warfare Development Group (DEVGRU / SEAL Team 6).

Operating in the shadows with DEVGRU's Silver Squadron, Thomas deployed repeatedly into the most contested hot zones in the world. He was the quintessential quiet professional: intensely capable, humble, and fiercely devoted to the men to his left and right.

On August 18, 2010, during a high-stakes night raid against an insurgent compound in eastern Afghanistan, Chief Thomas was fatally struck by enemy small-arms fire while leading from the front. He was 33 years old. His service was recognized with the Silver Star, the Bronze Star with Valor, and the Purple Heart.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

One of my teammates gets over to me. The look on his face said everything: Nick’s not going to make it.

I looked at him and said, ‘Listen man, go work on someone you can save. I am in the expectant category here in triage. Don’t waste your time, precious seconds, and resources on me, because I’m done here.’”

His teammates refused to quit on him. They cranked tourniquets onto his mangled leg, stabilized him under fire, and got him on a medevac bird.

Not only did Nick survive having his leg amputated above the knee, but he also refused medical retirement. Imagine being strapped into a seat facing backward, in the windowless belly of a propeller plane on the deck of an aircraft carrier in the middle of the ocean. A single pair of Greyhounds could move a million pounds of cargo and 5,000 passengers in one deployment. Quietly, it kept the world's most powerful warships running.

After six decades, the Greyhound flew its last flight earlier in 2026, retired to a museum in Pensacola and replaced by the CMV-22B Osprey. "It's very sad to me," said the pilot of that final flight, "but I feel a lot of satisfaction that we did it safely."

The lone Navy corpsman who sprinted into a burning building to save six coalition soldiers.

On the night of March 12 in northern Iraq, an enemy one-way attack drone detonated roughly 25 meters from the living quarters of Navy Hospital Corpsman 2nd Class (HM2) Jajuan Hernandez.

Serving as the sole U.S. medic at the outpost while attached to the 2nd Marine Raider Battalion (MARSOC), Hernandez grabbed his weapon, body armor, and trauma bag, sprinting directly toward the fire amidst secondary ammunition explosions.

He arrived at a demolished berthing area to find seven critically wounded French coalition soldiers lying in the dark.

Despite severe language barriers, Hernandez directed nearby Marine Raiders to assist with bandaging and hypothermia blankets while personally executing advanced, life-saving battlefield surgical procedures:

Blunt finger thoracostomy and needle decompression (making incisions to vent air pressure around collapsed lungs and the heart).

Administering fresh whole blood intraosseously ("via the bone").

Applying tourniquets and chest seals under active secondary cook-offs.

 Acting Surgeon General of the Navy Rear Adm. Matthew Case credited Hernandez's quick thinking with directly saving the lives of six French soldiers until medical evacuations could arrive.

In late September, Hernandez was officially presented with the Armed Services YMCA's prestigious 2026 Angels of the Battlefield Award in Washington, D.C.

How much has the war with Iran cost the United States? It is a simple question with a surprisingly slippery answer.

The most recent official estimate, from US Central Command, puts the figure at just over 47 billion dollars. The largest cost by far is munitions, nearly 30 billion dollars' worth expended since the fighting began in February 2026, plus about 7.6 billion for air operations and 1.5 billion for the Navy-led blockade of Iran.

But even that number leaves things out. It does not include the cost of repairing the widespread damage done to US bases hit by Iranian attacks, which the Pentagon says it cannot fully estimate yet. That is a big reason the estimates vary so much: an earlier public figure put the cost around 25 billion, while US officials told CBS and CNN the real total was already closer to 40 to 50 billion, and some projections run higher still once long-term costs like replacing munitions are counted.

None of the numbers is exactly wrong. They are measuring different things over different timeframes. The honest answer to what the Iran war has cost is a range, not a single figure: at least 47 billion by the military's own count, and quite possibly more once the full picture comes in.

According to defense officials and diplomatic sources, U.S. defense leadership has privately urged several European allies—particularly frontline Baltic nations like Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia—to "cool" their public warnings regarding the threat of direct military conflict with Moscow.

Frontline European Allies argue that sounding the alarm and showing relentless public defiance is the only deterrent Moscow respects, warning that softening rhetoric projects weakness.

Pictured on the left is a young Mike Vining during his time as an Explosive Ordnance Disposal specialist in the Vietnam War. The photo was taken just before Christmas 1970 at Tay Ninh, during the cleanup of an ammunition bunker filled with MK 45 aircraft flares, 20mm rounds, and 40mm M406 grenades. Vining ended the job covered in fiberglass from the burned out flares, while South Vietnamese Army soldiers worked nearby trying to pull the parachutes out of them.

This rare look shows an Uruguayan military member holding an iconic, combat-proven M1A1 Thompson submachine gun—a weapon that first saw action on the battlefields of World War II over 80 years ago.   

Originally acquired through mid-20th-century U.S. military aid programs, the heavy, milled-steel M1A1 Thompson served as a frontline submachine gun in Uruguay until the mid-1980s, when it was officially replaced by the 9mm Argentine-made FMK-3 submachine gun. 

Rather than melting down or destroying obsolete small arms when new rifles arrive, the Uruguayan military has historically maintained a policy of preserving older weapons in deep-storage armories. Because of this, classic firearms like the M1A1 Thompson, M1 Garand, and M1 Carbine occasionally resurface for specialized familiarity training, reserve exercises, or ceremonial duties. 

Weighing in at roughly 10 pounds unloaded and firing the hard-hitting .45 ACP cartridge at 700+ rounds per minute, the simplified wartime M1A1 design is practically indestructible—proving that good steel and timeless engineering never truly go out of style.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

Can a dedicated 26-Marine Scout Platoon fully replace the legendary Scout Sniper platoons and give infantry commanders the ultimate eyes and ears on the modern battlefield? 

The U.S. Marine Corps’ newest primary infantry career field—the 0315 Marine Scout—is officially in effect, establishing a dedicated reconnaissance and surveillance pipeline on the heels of the Corps' controversial decision to phase out traditional Scout Sniper platoons in 2023.   

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

In 1978, an 11-year-old kid sent hand-drawn missile blueprints to the Pentagon—and instead of tossing them in the trash, the Office of Naval Research gave him an official, deadpan engineering breakdown.

The Navy’s Patent Counsel actually took the time to review the submission:

The Concept: A winged, ramjet-powered missile armed with a nuclear warhead, machine guns, and sub-missiles.

The Navy's Debrief: They politely explained that ramjets require a booster to hit supersonic speed before ignition, pointed out that oversized wings create too much drag at hypersonic velocity, and noted that the Army was already testing clustered sub-munitions.

The Verdict: The Navy formally declined to adopt the platform, but enclosed real unclassified research on solid-fuel ramjet missiles so the kid could study up.

That’s how you handle curious minds. No condescension, just cold aerospace physics and encouragement from the Fleet.

Imagine pitching nuclear-armed, ramjet-driven micro-missiles from your bedroom floor and getting a typed letter back from the Chief of Naval Research. Elite era.

Operators from the Army's SMU in Mogadishu, Somalia, in 1993. They deployed as part of Task Force Ranger alongside the 75th Ranger Regiment and the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment, with the mission of capturing the leadership of Mohamed Farrah Aidid's militia.

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

“DON’T WASTE YOUR TIME ON ME. I AM IN THE EXPECTANT CATEGORY. I’M DONE HERE.” — Green Beret Warrant Officer Nick Lavery on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

My training tells me: move to cover, eliminate the threat. But six feet in front of me is one of our infantry uplift soldiers—young kid, first deployment, fresh out of basic. He’s 15 feet in front of a guy shooting a machine gun in his general direction, frozen like a deer in the headlights.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

One of my teammates gets over to me. The look on his face said everything: Nick’s not going to make it.

I looked at him and said, ‘Listen man, go work on someone you can save. I am in the expectant category here in triage. Don’t waste your time, precious seconds, and resources on me, because I’m done here.’”

His teammates refused to quit on him. They cranked tourniquets onto his mangled leg, stabilized him under fire, and got him on a medevac bird.

Not only did Nick survive having his leg amputated above the knee, but he also refused medical retirement. He underwent grueling rehab, relearned how to shoot, sprint, and clear rooms on a carbon-fiber prosthetic, and became the first active-duty Green Beret in history to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee.

Ordering your brothers to leave you behind to save others while you bleed out from a severed femoral artery is the ultimate definition of selfless service.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. The President of the United States of America, authorized by Title 10, Section 8742, U.S.C., awarded the Air Force Cross to Captain Barry F. Crawford, Jr., for extraordinary heroism in military operations against an armed enemy of the United States as Special Tactics Officer of the 21st Special Tactics Squadron, in action near Laghman Province, Afghanistan, on 4 May 2010. On that date, while attached to Army Special Forces Operational Detachment Alpha and their Afghan partner force, Captain Crawford conducted a helicopter assault into Hendor Village. Upon landing, Captain Crawford received reports that multiple groups of armed enemy were maneuvering into prepared fighting positions in the high ground around the village. As the assault force initiated clearance operations, they began to receive a high volume of accurate machine gun and sniper fire from an enemy force well over 100 fighters. As the assault force was attacked, Captain Crawford took decisive action to save the lives of three wounded Afghan soldiers and evacuate two Afghan soldiers killed in action. Recognizing that the wounded Afghan soldiers would die without evacuation to definitive care, Captain Crawford took decisive action and ran out into the open in an effort to guide the helicopter to the landing zone. Once the pilot had eyes on his position, Captain Crawford remained exposed, despite having one of his radio antennas shot off mere inches from theirhis face, while he vectored in the aircraft. Acting without hesitation, Captain Crawford then bounded across open terrain, engaged enemy positions with his assault rifle and called in AH-64 strafe attacks to defeat the ambush allowing the aid-and-litter teams to move toward the casualties. While the casualties were being moved the team’s exposed position once again came under attack from two enemy trucks that had moved into the area and were threatening the medical evacuation landing zone. As one of the aid-and-litter teams was pinned down by enemy fire, and the medical evacuation helicopter took direct hits from small arms fire, it departed with only four casualties leaving one wounded Afghan soldier on the ground. Captain Crawford developed, coordinated, and executed a plan to suppress the enemy, enabling the helicopter to return to the hot landing zone to retrieve the last casualty. While Captain Crawford’s element exfiltrated the village, the assault force conducted a two kilometer movement over steep terrain with little to no cover. During this movement the ground force commander and Captain Crawford’s element were ambushed and pinned down in the open from multiple enemy fighting positions, some as close as 150 meters away. Without regard for his own life, Captain Crawford moved alone across open terrain in the kill zone to locate and engage enemy positions with his assault riffle while directing AH-64 30-mm. strafe attacks. Continuing to move the team further over 1.5 kilometers of steep terrain with minimal cover, Captain Crawford again engaged the enemy with his assault rifle while integrating AH-64s and F-15E’s in a coordinated air-to-ground attack plan that included strafing runs along with 500 and 2,0000-pound bomb and Hellfire missile strikes. Throughout the course of the ten hour firefight, Captain Crawford braved effective enemy fire and consciously placed himself at grave risk on four occasions while controlling over 33 aircraft and more than 40 air strikes on a well-trained and well-prepared enemy force. His selfless actions and expert airpower employment neutralized a numerically superior enemy force and enabled friendly elements to exfiltrate the area without massive casualties. Through his extraordinary heroism, superb airmanship, and aggressiveness in the face of the enemy, Captain Crawford has reflected great credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.

MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. (5/18/2012) – Corporal Christopher B. Farias, 1st Battalion, 11th Marine Regiment, was awarded the nation's second highest award for bravery during a ceremony here, May 18.

Under Secretary of the Navy Robert Work presented the Navy Cross to Farias for heroic actions while serving as an assistant squad leader in the Kajaki district of Afghanistan on Oct. 5, 2010.

After Farias, a native of La Porte, Texas, arrived in Afghanistan, the commanding officer pulled the Marines together and mentioned they would protect the Kajaki Dam and relieve British forces at the front line.

“To find out that we're surrounded in three different areas by Taliban fighters, that's telling me that we're definitely on our own on this one,” Farias explained.

Farias was excited to do infantry missions because he had experience in Iraq with foot patrols and security and felt the Marines in his squad were well trained and confident in their abilities to complete their mission on the northern frontier of the Marines' battlespace in Kajaki.

During the night of the fight, Farias requested to go on the mission because he enjoyed patrolling, he said. The Marines planned to set up an ambush against enemy forces moving throughout the area.

While preparing for the attack, the Marines received reports that enemy fighters called for reinforcements, including a “special weapon,” a 73-millimeter recoilless rifle. The rounds are larger than the rounds of some mortar systems.

Farias and the squad heard an explosion and received enemy fire from three positions in a vicious ambush. Several Marines lay wounded by the recoilless rifle, and insurgent forces adjusted their fires and continued to shoot into the Marines' position.
 

“These guys were tactically and strategically smart,” said Farias. They were well trained. To have guys who can fight just like you... they know how to maneuver, they know how to set you up for a proper ambush... to fight an enemy like that, it's pretty insane.”

Farias suffered a concussion and fragmentation wounds in the neck and shoulder and received hasty treatment for his wounds before directing medical care for the other Marines. After securing the wounded, Farias climbed to a rooftop and controlled the fire of the machine guns to suppress enemy positions.

The suppressive fires kept the enemy down and allowed the squad to treat the wounded, clear a landing zone, and evacuate the casualties. Farias remained with his squad until an airstrike ended the engagement.

Afterward, Farias walked more than 2,000 meters back to a ground evacuation site. His neck was bleeding, and he felt drained due to blood loss, he remembered.

“As we were walking back, that's when I started feeling every bit of pain possible,” recounted Farias. “I ended up realizing my right arm would not move. I could not move it to save my life if I wanted to.”
Farias was recommended for a Silver Star, which was upgraded to a Navy Cross. The Marines of 1st Battalion, 11th Marine Regiment formed on the parade deck with M777 lightweight howitzers on display. Farias said he was honored to receive the award on behalf of his Marines and the unit.

“I don't see it as actually for me,” Farias said. “I see it as for India Battery, but for me to stand there and be a representation for India Battery for that award... it's a shocker.”

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

“DON’T WASTE YOUR TIME ON ME. I AM IN THE EXPECTANT CATEGORY. I’M DONE HERE.” — Green Beret Warrant Officer Nick Lavery on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

My training tells me: move to cover, eliminate the threat. But six feet in front of me is one of our infantry uplift soldiers—young kid, first deployment, fresh out of basic. He’s 15 feet in front of a guy shooting a machine gun in his general direction, frozen like a deer in the headlights.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

One of my teammates gets over to me. The look on his face said everything: Nick’s not going to make it.

I looked at him and said, ‘Listen man, go work on someone you can save. I am in the expectant category here in triage. Don’t waste your time, precious seconds, and resources on me, because I’m done here.’”

His teammates refused to quit on him. They cranked tourniquets onto his mangled leg, stabilized him under fire, and got him on a medevac bird.

Not only did Nick survive having his leg amputated above the knee, but he also refused medical retirement. He underwent grueling rehab, relearned how to shoot, sprint, and clear rooms on a carbon-fiber prosthetic, and became the first active-duty Green Beret in history to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee.

After leading his platoon through a fierce onslaught with enemy fire pounding them from every direction, 1st Lt. Neil Prakash went back in for more.

For Prakash, June 24, 2004, began with him and two of his soldiers manning an observation point on Blue Babe Highway in two shifts from midnight to 7 a.m. “When we came in (to Forward Operating Base Scunion) at 7, we thought we were done,” Prakash said. “We were smoked after being out there all night.”

Instead, Prakash's crew was sent back out to Blue Babe Highway after there were reports of 25 to 30 insurgents on the roadway, which was a trouble spot for improvised explosive devices.

Three hours later, Prakash returned to FOB Scunion and learned that his entire company, Company A, was going to Baqouba, where the city was under siege.

With Prakash's 1st Platoon in the lead, the company headed into Baqouba with the mission of securing two bridges in the city. If successful, his platoon would set up a blocking position to prevent the enemy from reinforcing.

“When we learned we were going in, we were really pumped up,” Prakash said. At about 11 a.m., the company was driving south in Baqouba with Prakash's tank taking the point. “It was very quiet, like a ghost town,” Prakash said. “There was just nobody there.”Suddenly a call from the operations center warned that, based on intelligence from unmanned aerial flights, insurgents were in groups of four; they were well-trained and they were going to stand and fight, Prakash said.

It wasn't long thereafter that Prakash heard an explosion behind his tank. A rocket-propelled grenade fired from a house on the left hit his tank. 

“We fired the main gun at the house and there was just this big giant blob of a hole in the house,” he said. “They were everywhere, running up to within 30 meters of the tank shooting RPGs at us.” As the lead vehicle, Prakash and his gunner and driver were the main target in the ambush of IEDs and rocket-propelled grenades.

His tank took several hits without much damage, but eventually one RPG took out the tank's navigation system while another hit the turret, making it impossible to rotate. The tank was hit by seven RPGs as well as multiple IED blasts. Prakash maneuvered the entire vehicle in order to engage the enemy with the main weapon system and .50-caliber machinegun. 

“Someone told me right afterward that we were fighting for an hour,” Prakash said. “I thought it was more like 15 minutes. Everything happened so fast.” Prakash's tank returned to FOB Scunion for more ammo and to have the damaged turret repaired. He volunteered to go back into battle to secure and hold the two bridges. The insurgents had fled. 

“He was incredible,” said Spc. John Langford, Prakash's loader in the battle. “He kept us in line and kept us calm. I couldn't have chosen a better tank commander or platoon leader for what we experienced that day.” 

Prakash, who was born in India and raised in Syracuse, N.Y., earned a Silver Star for his actions. He was personally credited with the destruction of eight enemy strong points, one enemy resupply vehicle, and multiple dismounted enemy fighters.

Long before historical milestones or public acclaim, operators on the ground faced grueling, unglamorous days on the ridgelines—managing casualties, combat stress, and severe physical depletion under constant threat.

This rare look shows an Uruguayan military member holding an iconic, combat-proven M1A1 Thompson submachine gun—a weapon that first saw action on the battlefields of World War II over 80 years ago.   

Originally acquired through mid-20th-century U.S. military aid programs, the heavy, milled-steel M1A1 Thompson served as a frontline submachine gun in Uruguay until the mid-1980s, when it was officially replaced by the 9mm Argentine-made FMK-3 submachine gun. 

Rather than melting down or destroying obsolete small arms when new rifles arrive, the Uruguayan military has historically maintained a policy of preserving older weapons in deep-storage armories. Because of this, classic firearms like the M1A1 Thompson, M1 Garand, and M1 Carbine occasionally resurface for specialized familiarity training, reserve exercises, or ceremonial duties. 

Weighing in at roughly 10 pounds unloaded and firing the hard-hitting .45 ACP cartridge at 700+ rounds per minute, the simplified wartime M1A1 design is practically indestructible—proving that good steel and timeless engineering never truly go out of style.

CW4 Keith Yoakum, awarded Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

Citation of Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

CW4 Keith Yoakum,
Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment
1st Air Cavalry Brigade, Multi-National Division (Baghdad)

CW4 Keith Yoakum distinguished himself by gallantry and courage at the risk of his own life above and beyond the call of duty as an AH-64D Longbow Apache Pilot-in Command while providing cover for his wingman on 2 February 2007 during aerial combat against a deliberate helicopter ambush site.

The previous two weeks in the Baghdad area of operations witnessed four separate attacks on coalition aircraft, resulting in the loss of 19 lives and the destruction of one AH-64D Longbow Apache, one UH-60 Blackhawk, and two Department of Defense contracted helicopters. CW4 Yoakum was the first responder to the UH-60 crash site and was intimately familiar with the enemy's helicopter ambush tactics.

CW4 Yoakum was the Pilot-in-Command of the trail aircraft in a flight of two AH-64D Longbow Apache helicopters as they departed on a reconnaissance mission in support of four separate ground brigades on the morning of 2 February 2007. Just when the Apache team began reconnaissance of a test fire area, waves of red tracers and heavy machine gun fire burst into the sky from multiple directions and raked the Apaches. The tracer fire immediately engulfed CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and riddled his fuselage. The enemy had established a deadly kill zone comprised of multiple heavy machine gun and anti-aircraft gun positions. With its interlocking fields of heavy anti-aircraft fire, the enemy ambush site was similar to the earlier ambush site that had downed a UH-60—the same UH-60 that CW4 Yoakum had responded to 13 days earlier, thus familiarizing him with the lethality of the enemy's tactics.

CW4 Yoakum immediately radioed his lead aircraft to maneuver it away from the direction of fire. As the lead aircraft broke hard to the right, the enemy responded, shifting its fire away from CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and toward the lead aircraft. CW4 Yoakum warned the lead helicopter announcing “now you're taking fire!” and the two aircraft broke left to escape the deadly kill zone.

Despite the damage to his aircraft, CW4 Yoakum took personal charge of the team amid the melee of bullets, calmed his lead aircraft, and steered the team out of the kill zone. The team raced to the north to separate from the enemy force and to acquire standoff range to assess the situation. Immediately after their turn to the north, CW4 Yoakum announced that he had “lost utility hydraulics,” a condition that requires the pilot to land the aircraft immediately at the nearest clear landing area. As the senior maintenance test pilot in the company, a prior instructor to other maintenance test pilots, and a Master Army Aviator with almost 5000 flight hours, CW4 Yoakum instantly understood the gravity of his Apache's emergency condition. Furthermore, CW4 Yoakum recognized that the loss of hydraulic pressure prevented him from employing his aircraft's main gun. As a result, he would have to use the aircraft's 2.75 inch rockets from a fixed position, requiring him to skillfully maneuver his crippled aircraft to accurately employ the rockets against the enemy.

The team continued northbound and after approximately two minutes no longer had tracers whipping by their windscreens. Once clear of the immediate threat, CW4 Yoakum had the opportunity to fly his critically damaged aircraft back to the airfield or land in the open desert to conduct an emergency extraction of his crew on his wingman's aircraft. He again announced “we've got no utility hydraulics left.” Still, despite the cockpit warnings and CW4 Yoakum's own recognition of his grave situation, he never considered leaving his wingman and knew this enemy would kill again if left on the battlefield. The enemy had a distinct advantage as a result of their concealed position among the numerous canals and irrigation ditches in the surrounding countryside. Despite the fierce danger inherent in pressing the attack, CW4 Yoakum radioed his wingman that “I can put rockets in” and continued to plan the route back into the withering fire of the enemy's ambush site to destroy the enemy's anti-aircraft positions.

CW4 Yoakum's instructions to his lead aircraft were simple: “you find them, we've got you covered.” CW4 Yoakum knew that his Apache team had a sliver of an opportunity to engage and destroy the enemy before they blended into the Iraqi countryside. The team decided to search the ambush area in a cloverleaf pattern, thereby performing a sweep of the area from all directions until they were able to locate the anti-aircraft guns. Despite his aircraft's crippled condition and the knowledge of the volume of fire that would again rake his aircraft at the ambush site, CW4 Yoakum was determined to cover his wingman as they searched for targets and eliminated the enemy position which was certain to be set up again at a different time and place to destroy coalition aircraft.

Approximately two minutes after the initial ambush had crippled CW4 Yoakum's Apache, the lead aircraft, acting on CW4 Yoakum's instructions, turned south to begin their search for the enemy ambush site. Despite the deteriorating condition of his own aircraft, CW4 Yoakum announced “I'm going to climb up and cover you from high and we're gonna work on rockets.” As he continued losing critical hydraulic pressure, CW4 Yoakum determined that his degraded weapons systems necessitated that he climb to altitude and then dive his damaged aircraft directly at the enemy to provide effective rocket fire. Only by diving from a higher altitude directly toward the enemy position could he provide precise rocket fire for his wingman while focusing his fires solely on the enemy and away from the surrounding villages and homes in the Iraqi countryside. With unmatched skill and extraordinary courage, CW4 Yoakum began his climb to posture his crippled aircraft in a diving position, knowing full well that his climb would give the enemy gunners a clearer line of sight and more time with which to engage his aircraft as he maneuvered back towards the ambush site.

CW4 Yoakum's focus on the destruction of the enemy's anti-aircraft guns caused him to demand as much from his aircraft as he did from himself, but his dying Apache was not able to sustain its altitude. As the Apache team made a second inbound run to the ambush area utilizing their cloverleaf pattern, the lead Apache radioed to CW4 Yoakum to ensure that he was still with them. After transmitting several radio calls and receiving no response, the lead aircraft began a left turn and acquired CW4 Yoakum's aircraft. After flying for almost four minutes in a critical state, CW4 Yoakum's Apache had succumbed to its battle damage and was engulfed in a blazing fire on the ground following a crash that had instantly killed CW4 Yoakum and his copilot.

CW4 Yoakum acted to protect his wingman and destroy an enemy anti-aircraft position designed to produce the continued loss of coalition aircraft. His decision to knowingly risk his life to cover his lead aircraft, despite having the opportunity to land or return to the airfield, put the accomplishment of his mission and the protection of his comrades over his own personal safety. His personal bravery and uncommon valor at the risk of his own life reflects great credit upon himself, the 1st Air Cavalry Brigade, the First Cavalry Division and the Multinational Division-Baghdad, and the United States Army.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

Can a dedicated 26-Marine Scout Platoon fully replace the legendary Scout Sniper platoons and give infantry commanders the ultimate eyes and ears on the modern battlefield? 

The U.S. Marine Corps’ newest primary infantry career field—the 0315 Marine Scout—is officially in effect, establishing a dedicated reconnaissance and surveillance pipeline on the heels of the Corps' controversial decision to phase out traditional Scout Sniper platoons in 2023.   

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.
